procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 13.08.2015 passed by the High Court of Assam in Criminal Revision Petition No.6 of 2014.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The State preferred Criminal Revision Petition No.6 of 2014 before the High Court, challenging the Special Court's order dated 26.08.2014 (dismissing SR (PCA) No.8 of 2014 and holding the second charge sheet was barred by double jeopardy) and the earlier order dated 12.09.2013. The High Court dismissed the revision petition, affirming the Special Court's order that the second charge sheet with fresh sanction could not be entertained. The High Court also held that the revision petition against the order dated 12.09.2013 was barred by limitation.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State, aggrieved by the High Court's order, approached the Supreme Court by filing Criminal Appeal No. 1322 of 2018. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment, and directed the Special Court to take cognizance of the charge sheet dated 30.01.2014 and proceed in accordance with law.

issue.issue_text: Whether Section 19(3) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, prohibits a Special Judge from dismissing a prosecution at any stage for want of a valid sanction.

facts: The issue before the court was the correct interpretation of Section 19(3) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.
Specifically, the question was whether this provision prevents a Special Judge (the trial court) from dismissing a case at any point because the sanction to prosecute is invalid.
law: Section 19(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, requires a valid sanction from a competent authority before a court can take cognizance of an offence against a public servant.

Section 19(3) states that no finding, sentence, or order passed by a Special Judge shall be reversed or altered by a court in appeal or revision on the ground of an error, omission, or irregularity in the sanction, unless it has resulted in a failure of justice.
The competence of a court to try an accused public servant depends on the existence of a valid sanction.
application: The Supreme Court explained that Section 19(3) is a prohibition directed at higher courts (appellate or revisional courts), not at the Special Judge (the trial court).
The provision's purpose is to prevent a concluded trial from being overturned on the technical ground of a faulty sanction, unless a real 'failure of justice' has occurred.

The Court clarified that Section 19(3) has "no application to proceedings before the Special Judge." Therefore, the Special Judge is not bound by this provision and is free to examine the validity of a sanction at any stage.
If the Special Judge finds that the sanction is invalid, they have the power to discharge the accused and dismiss the prosecution, as the court's competence to proceed depends on a valid sanction.
The 'failure of justice' test is to be applied by the appellate or revisional court when reviewing an order, not by the Special Judge when initially deciding on the validity of the sanction.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that Section 19(3) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, does not prohibit a Special Judge from dismissing a prosecution at any stage for want of a valid sanction. The prohibition in that subsection applies only to appellate and revisional courts reviewing a decision already made by the Special Judge.

issue.issue_text: Whether a subsequent prosecution, after a prior dismissal for want of a valid sanction, is barred by the principle of double jeopardy.

facts: A case was registered against the respondent-accused under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, and the Indian Penal Code.
The Special Court discharged the accused and closed the case because the sanction for prosecution was found to be invalid.
Subsequently, the Governor granted a new, valid sanction for prosecution.
The prosecution then submitted a supplementary charge sheet along with the new sanction to reopen the case.
The Special Court and the High Court dismissed this new charge sheet, holding that it was barred by the principle of double jeopardy.
law: The principle of double jeopardy is enshrined in Article 20(2) of the Constitution of India and Section 300(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC).
Article 20(2) states that no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once.
Section 300(1) CrPC specifies that for this bar to apply, a person must have been previously 'tried' by a competent court and either 'convicted or acquitted' of the offence.
An invalid sanction for prosecution is a procedural defect. There is no bar for the competent authority to issue a proper, valid sanction after a case is dismissed on this ground.
Proceedings are not vitiated by an error or irregularity in the sanction unless it has caused a failure of justice.
application: The Supreme Court analyzed the nature of the initial dismissal. It found that the respondent was not 'tried' in a full-fledged trial, nor was he 'convicted or acquitted'.
Instead, the respondent was 'discharged' before the trial even commenced, solely due to a technical and procedural defect: the lack of a valid sanction.
The Court reasoned that since the essential conditions for invoking double jeopardy (a prior trial resulting in conviction or acquittal) were not met, the principle could not be applied.
The initial dismissal was due to an 'invalidity attached to the prosecution' and not a decision on the merits of the case.
Therefore, obtaining a valid sanction and filing a fresh/supplementary charge sheet was permissible and did not cause any prejudice or failure of justice to the respondent.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the subsequent prosecution was barred by double jeopardy. It held that the principle does not apply when an accused is merely discharged due to a procedural defect like an invalid sanction before the trial begins, as this does not constitute a trial, conviction, or acquittal. Consequently, the prosecution was permitted to file a fresh charge sheet after obtaining a valid sanction.

issue.issue_text: Whether Sections 19(3) and 19(4) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, permit a challenge to the validity of a sanction order during the proceedings.

law.fact_text: Section 19(3) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, prohibits an appellate or revisional court from reversing or altering a finding, sentence, or order of a Special Judge due to an error, omission, or irregularity in the sanction, unless it has resulted in a failure of justice.
relevant_text: A careful reading of sub-section (3) to Section 19 would show that the same interdicts reversal or alteration of any finding, sentence or order passed by a Special Judge, on the ground that the sanction order suffers from an error, omission or irregularity, unless of course the court before whom such finding, sentence or order is challenged in appeal or revision is of the opinion that a failure of justice has occurred by reason of such error, omission or irregularity.

law.fact_text: The prohibition in Section 19(3) applies to higher courts (appellate or revisional) and does not apply to the proceedings before the Special Judge (the trial court).
relevant_text: What is noteworthy is that sub-section (3) has no application to proceedings before the Special Judge...

Sub-section (3), in our opinion, postulates a prohibition against a higher court reversing an order passed by the Special Judge on the ground of any defect, omission or irregularity in the order of sanction. It does not forbid a Special Judge from passing an order at whatever stage of the proceedings holding that the prosecution is not maintainable for want of a valid order sanctioning the same.

law.fact_text: The validity of a sanction order can be challenged at any stage of the proceedings before the trial court.
relevant_text: The question regarding validity of such sanction can be raised at any stage of the proceedings.

law.fact_text: If a sanction is found to be invalid by the trial court, it can discharge the accused.
relevant_text: In case the sanction is found to be invalid the court can discharge the accused...

...the Special Judge, who is free to pass an order discharging the accused, if he is of the opinion that a valid order sanctioning prosecution of the accused had not been produced as required under Section 19(1).

application.fact_text: The Court analyzed Section 19(3) and determined that its purpose is to prevent concluded trials from being easily overturned by higher courts on the technical ground of a defective sanction, unless a failure of justice is shown.
relevant_text: The rationale underlying the provision obviously is that if the trial has proceeded to conclusion and resulted in a finding or sentence, the same should not be lightly interfered with by the appellate or the revisional court simply because there was some omission, error or irregularity in the order sanctioning the prosecution under Section 19(1).

application.fact_text: The Court explicitly distinguished the role of the trial court (Special Judge) from that of the appellate or revisional courts. It found that the restrictions in Section 19(3) are directed at the higher courts, not the trial court.
relevant_text: Sub-section (3) has no application to proceedings before the Special Judge...
It does not forbid a Special Judge from passing an order at whatever stage of the proceedings holding that the prosecution is not maintainable for want of a valid order sanctioning the same.

application.fact_text: By reading Sections 19(3) and 19(4) together, the Court concluded that the law itself anticipates that a challenge to the sanction's validity can and should be made during the trial proceedings.
relevant_text: Suffice it to say, that a conjoint reading of sub-sections 19(3) and (4) leaves no manner of doubt that the said provisions envisage a challenge to the validity of the order of sanction or the validity of the proceedings including finding, sentence or order passed by

application.fact_text: The Court noted that Section 19(4) supports this interpretation by requiring the appellate/revisional court to consider whether the objection to the sanction 'could and should have been raised at an early stage,' implying that the trial stage is the appropriate time for such a challenge.
relevant_text: This is, in our opinion, sufficiently evident even from the language employed in sub-section (4) according to which the appellate or the revisional court shall, while examining whether the error, omission or irregularity in the sanction had occasioned in any failure of justice, have regard to the fact whether the objection could and should have been raised at an early stage.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that Sections 19(3) and 19(4) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, do permit a challenge to the validity of a sanction order at any stage during the proceedings before the Special Judge (the trial court). The Court clarified that the restrictions imposed by these sections, which limit overturning a decision based on a faulty sanction unless there is a 'failure of justice', apply only to appellate and revisional courts after a trial has concluded. The trial court itself is not forbidden from examining the validity of the sanction and can discharge the accused if the sanction is found to be invalid.

arguments.issue_text: Whether Section 19(3) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, prohibits a Special Judge from dismissing a prosecution at any stage for want of a valid sanction.
appellant_arguments: The appellant likely argued that Section 19(3) does not prohibit a Special Judge from dismissing a prosecution for want of a valid sanction. A valid sanction is a prerequisite for taking cognizance, and if the sanction is found to be invalid at any stage, the court can discharge the accused or dismiss the prosecution.
respondent_arguments: The respondent likely argued that Section 19(3) acts as a bar, preventing a court from dismissing a prosecution on the grounds of an invalid sanction during the trial. They would have contended that any error in the sanction can only be considered at the final stage or by an appellate/revisional court to see if it has caused a failure of justice.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a subsequent prosecution, after a prior dismissal for want of a valid sanction, is barred by the principle of double jeopardy.
appellant_arguments: The appellant likely argued that a dismissal based on the absence of a valid sanction is not an acquittal on the merits of the case. Therefore, the principle of double jeopardy does not apply, and a fresh prosecution can be initiated after obtaining a valid sanction.
respondent_arguments: The respondent likely argued that a subsequent prosecution is barred by the principle of double jeopardy, as the accused has already faced trial and the proceedings were terminated.

arguments.issue_text: Whether Sections 19(3) and 19(4) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, permit a challenge to the validity of a sanction order during the proceedings.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that a conjoint reading of sub-sections 19(3) and 19(4) allows for a challenge to the validity of the sanction order during the proceedings. The language in sub-section (4), which states that an appellate or revisional court should consider whether 'the objection could and should have been raised at an early stage,' explicitly envisages that such challenges can and should be made during the trial itself.
respondent_arguments: The respondent likely argued that Sections 19(3) and 19(4) are intended to prevent trials from being stalled on technical grounds. Therefore, any challenge to the validity of a sanction should only be considered at the appellate or revisional stage, and only if a failure of justice is demonstrated.

cases.principle: A challenge to the validity of a sanction order must be considered based on a conjoint reading of Section 19(3) and (4). The court must determine if the error, omission, or irregularity in the sanction has occasioned a failure of justice, and have regard to whether the objection could and should have been raised at an earlier stage.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The prohibition under Section 19(3) against a higher court reversing an order on the ground of a defect in sanction does not prevent a Special Judge, at any stage of the proceedings, from holding that a prosecution is not maintainable for want of a valid sanction.
obiter: A conjoint reading of sub-sections 19(3) and (4) shows that the provisions envisage a challenge to the validity of the sanction order.
When examining if an error in sanction has caused a failure of justice, an appellate or revisional court must consider whether the objection could and should have been raised at an earlier stage.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Section 19(3) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, does not prohibit a Special Judge from dismissing a prosecution at any stage for want of a valid sanction. The prohibition in Section 19(3) applies to appellate or revisional courts reviewing a concluded trial, not to the Special Judge during the proceedings. A dismissal based on an invalid sanction is due to a fundamental error that invalidates the proceedings, is not an acquittal on the merits, and therefore does not bar a subsequent prosecution on the principle of double jeopardy once a valid sanction is obtained.
legal_tests_applied: Failure of Justice Test: An appellate or revisional court can only reverse or alter a finding, sentence, or order on the ground of an error, omission, or irregularity in the sanction if it is of the opinion that a failure of justice has in fact been occasioned thereby.

Fundamental Error Doctrine: When cognizance is taken without a valid sanction order, the error is so fundamental that it invalidates the proceedings conducted by the court, meaning there is no trial on the merits.
why_respondent_won: Section 19(3) does not forbid a Special Judge from dismissing a prosecution for want of a valid sanction; the prohibition is on a higher court reversing a final order on that ground. The court reasoned: 'Sub-section (3), in our opinion, postulates a prohibition against a higher court reversing an order passed by the Special Judge on the ground of any defect, omission or irregularity in the order of sanction. It does not forbid a Special Judge from passing an order at whatever stage of the proceedings holding that the prosecution is not maintainable for want of a valid order sanctioning the same.'

A subsequent prosecution after a dismissal for want of sanction is not barred by double jeopardy because the initial dismissal is not an acquittal on the merits. The court relied on precedent where 'when cognizance was taken by the Special Judge... there was no order sanctioning the prosecution with the result that the court could not have taken cognizance and that the error was so fundamental that it invalidated the proceedings conducted by the court.' A fresh prosecution after obtaining proper sanction is therefore permissible.

The validity of a sanction order can be challenged during the trial proceedings. The court found this evident from a 'conjoint reading of sub-sections 19(3) and (4),' noting that Section 19(4) requires higher courts to 'have regard to the fact whether the objection could and should have been raised at an early stage,' which presupposes that such an objection can be raised during the trial.
policy_considerations: The rationale behind Section 19(3) is to ensure that if a trial has proceeded to a conclusion and resulted in a finding or sentence, it should not be 'lightly interfered with by the appellate or the revisional court simply because there was some omission, error or irregularity in the order sanctioning the prosecution,' unless a failure of justice has occurred.
